title: Research Bite #67: To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Research Bite summarises Nicolas Hubner et al.'s study on grading, which first synthesizes 136 studies across motivation, assessment and feedback, and measurement research before reporting a quasi-experimental field trial of 2,342 German elementary students across 75 schools. Trial schools replaced numerical grades with standards-based competency grids and formative feedback; the researchers measured academic achievement, performance anxiety, and student well-being. The headline finding is a near-null result: abolishing grades produced no significant differences on most outcomes, with the single exception of a slight positive trend in mathematics interest for non-graded students. The theoretical framework draws on Self-Determination Theory and Cognitive Evaluation Theory, both of which predict grades act as an external pressure that can undermine intrinsic motivation — a prediction the data only weakly supports. Barton's take-home is that the centuries-old grading debate cannot be resolved by one study, but the evidence does not support strong claims in either direction.
points: A quasi-experimental trial of 2,342 German elementary students found abolishing grades produced no significant differences across most outcomes — including academic achievement and well-being — except a slight positive trend in mathematics interest.

The study's theoretical framework combines Self-Determination Theory, which predicts grades diminish intrinsic motivation as external pressure, with Cognitive Evaluation Theory, formalizing how external rewards affect autonomy and competence needs — yet the trial only weakly confirmed this prediction.
Standards-Based Grading did not reliably outperform traditional grading in this trial, a near-null finding that complicates strong advocacy claims on either side of the grading debate.

Removing grades without also building a genuine formative-feedback culture and providing teacher professional development is unlikely to change outcomes — the mechanism, not the absence of a grade, is what would have to do the work.
quotes: In trial schools, numerical marks were replaced with standards-based competency grids and formative feedback practices. The study measured a comprehensive suite of outcomes, including academic achievement, performance anxiety, and student well-being.
The study involved 2,342 elementary school students from 75 schools in Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany. This included 1,218 students in 35 trial schools and 1,124 students in 40 control schools.

First, it systematises the theoretical foundations of the grading debate into research on motivation, assessment, and measurement. Second, it provides rare, large-scale quasi-experimental evidence showing that abolishing grades yields neither broad educational improvements nor severe adverse effects.

For educators, the study indicates that simply removing grades does not automatically yield broad educational improvements, nor does it cause severe negative effects on student achievement, well-being, or performance anxiety.

Replacing traditional grades with low-stakes, formative alternatives—such as standards-based competency grids and learning-development meetings—can enhance students’ intrinsic motivation, particularly in subjects like mathematics.

Teachers should not expect immediate transformations in student outcomes, as effectively integrating new formative structures into daily instruction requires sustained effort. The full benefits of establishing these comprehensive classroom assessment cultures may only become observable much later in a student’s educational trajectory.

With the exception of mathematics interest, for which we found some evidence—though not consistently across all models—that students in schools that abolished grades might have benefited from this intervention, the results indicate no substantial overall differences between students with and without grades on any of the outcomes.
